title: Why our memories of 9/11 change – level 3
paragraphs: A flashbulb memory is a vivid recollection of learning about a major, highly emotional public event, such as the September 11 terror attacks. Although people feel absolute confidence in these memories, research shows they are not entirely accurate.

Memories are dynamic; each time a person retrieves one, the hippocampus updates it with new information from media or conversations. In fact, studies reveal that people alter roughly 40 percent of their personal details within a year. Unlike regular memories, emotional events activate the amygdala, which focuses attention and embeds the experience more strongly. These memories also strengthen social connection, because they create a shared sense of identity among groups.

Even prominent figures, including President George W. Bush, have famously mixed up the timeline of how they learned about the 9/11 attacks due to repeated exposure to news footage. Because modern media is highly fragmented, widespread flashbulb memories shared by whole nations may become less common in the future.
